comments.author: @rozsahegyi67
comments.text:
That woman focuses almost exclusively on what is arguably Alfa Romeo's most problematic product. The hybrid model has well-documented issues, and she should have done more research before buying it. The other models have proven to be far less troublesome.

It's also worth pointing out that the hybrid powertrain is a Dodge-derived product shared with the Dodge Hornet in its higher trim levels. If you choose the base 2.0-liter model instead, you'll generally encounter far fewer problems.

One of the biggest challenges with Alfa Romeo ownership isn't necessarily reliability—it's finding qualified technicians who know how to work on them. That's something every prospective buyer should consider before purchasing a vehicle they intend to keep long term.

People need to do their homework before making a major purchase. If you want luxury and the styling that comes with it, you also need to be prepared for the costs and ownership experience that accompany it.

If you're looking for honest owner feedback, you're better off visiting Alfa Romeo Facebook groups and owner forums, where you'll find a broad range of real-world experiences instead of relying on a single influencer whose presentation may be more about entertainment than balanced information.

If you want really good reviews of cars- The Car Nut, Car Wizard and Kirk Kreifels.

Heres a little breakdown for at least in California 


October 2026 is the California Combating Auto Retail Scams (CARS) Act, which becomes operative on October 1, 2026. This law targets auto dealership transparency, banning hidden fees, misrepresentations on financing, and adding a three-day cancellation right for vehicle purchases under $50,000. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Most users on Reddit agree that the act brings long-needed retail reforms to car buying. [1, 2]

Key Rules Under the CARS Act

Upfront Pricing: Dealers must clearly advertise the total price of a car, including all non-optional fees and destination charges (excluding only government fees). [1]

No Hidden Add-ons: Prohibits charging for add-on products or services that provide no clear benefit to the buyer or inflate the final cost deceptively. [1, 2]

Financing Honesty: Bars dealerships from misrepresenting loan terms, interest rates, or total financing costs. [1]

3-Day Return/Cancel Window: Requires a 3-day right to cancel or return a purchase or lease for vehicles priced under $50,000 (subject to specific mileage and condition restrictions). [1, 2]

replies.author: @yeppers7225
replies.text:
Yes TSB (temporary service bulletins) and recalls are typically covered by the manufacturer. Depending on the issue, many cover rental cars as well.  But there is also an inexpensive option to get rental cars under your car insurance as well. 

Lemon law rules vary by state, but only apply to brand new cars, meaning you are the first owner. Typically, in order for the lemon law to be applied, you must have had the exact same problem and have taken it to the dealership at least three separate times without a permanent resolution or fix. 

Before a car is actually replaced under the lemon law, the dealership service department are typically given a fourth attempt to fix the issue and if the issue resurfaces or cannot be fixed, the car can be replaced under the lemon law under state laws. Again, this process can vary by state, but this is typically how the process works. 

I have heard of very few cars that have actually been replaced by the lemon law, but it does happen.  Keeping documentation of everything is of paramount importance in order to prove the car is a lemon.  

This is a gross simplification of the actual process, but should give you a general idea of how it works. 

Hope this helps.
